title: Illness
hook: praying, seeking medicine, and trusting are not opposites

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion: the word holds suffering with someone, not fixing them from a distance. Your line was suffer with. Who did you stay beside yesterday, even for a minute? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

A hospital waiting room, late afternoon. On one chair, a woman holds a rosary in one hand and a list of her husband's medications in the other. Across from her, a man is reading the side effects on a pill bottle, then closing his eyes for a moment, lips moving. Nobody in that room thinks they have to choose. Yet the question comes up in some families: if you really trusted God, would you need the doctor? And if you go to the doctor, were the prayers just for show? Some very ordinary Bible verses speak to it. Today: illness.

Start with Jesus himself. When critics asked why he ate with sinners, he answered with a picture everyone understood: "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick." He used doctors as his example of help that's needed, not as a lack of faith. Then look at the letter of James. It tells the sick person to call the elders of the church: "let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Then go back to King Hezekiah, sick to the point of death. Isaiah brings him God's answer: "I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears." And then the prophet calls for something from the kitchen: "Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaster upon the boil." Prayer heard, and a poultice on the sore. Next, the letters to Timothy. Paul tells his young friend, in the King James words, "use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." Practical advice for a sick stomach, in the middle of scripture. And Paul names a companion in the letter to the Colossians: "Luke, the beloved physician." Tradition holds that this same Luke wrote one of the Gospels. A doctor, counted among the friends of the church. Last, what this doesn't promise. Christians who pray for healing don't all mean the same thing by it. Some expect dramatic recoveries and pray boldly for them. Others pray mostly for strength, peace and good doctors. Some churches anoint the sick as a sacrament; others lay on hands, or simply pray. What the texts keep doing is holding prayer and care together. Hands that pray, and hands that bandage. Both, not either.
screen: `A PRAYER HEARD, A POULTICE OF FIGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray and take your medicine. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing in your body that needs care right now: a pill you take, a sore back, a checkup you've been putting off, a night of sleep you keep skipping. Hold it without judging yourself. If you pray, you can name it to God, the way the sick in James are told to. Then decide on one plain, practical step you'll take for it this week. Hold both, side by side. The bell holds the time.
Illness. A weakness of the body that the Bible meets with prayer and with practical care, a physician and an anointing, held together.
Your line: both, not either. Today, take the practical step you named, a call, a pill, an appointment, and if you pray, pray as you do it. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Christians pray for the sick, by name in services and privately, while also seeking medical care; some churches anoint the sick with oil, following the letter of James, and Catholic and Orthodox churches keep this as a sacrament.

match.prompt: illness in the Bible — tap the pairs.

myth: Jesus treated needing a doctor as a lack of faith
he used the physician as his picture of needed help, and Paul calls Luke the beloved physician.
when King Hezekiah was sick, Isaiah called for a lump of figs
his prayer was heard, and the figs were laid on the boil as a plaster.
all Christians mean the same thing when they pray for healing
some pray boldly for recovery, others mainly for strength and good doctors; churches anoint, lay on hands, or simply pray.

fork.setup: you're one of the early Christians, and someone in your community is sick. according to the letter of James, what should they do?
options: keep quiet and wait it out alone.
call the elders, who pray and anoint them with oil.
avoid the church until they're well.
fork.reveal: James says the sick should call the elders, who pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord. illness is brought into the community, not hidden.

original.note: Greek: physician, the word in "they that are whole need not a physician" and in "Luke, the beloved physician."

trapdoor: what you thought: real faith means you don't need a doctor.
what it means: the Bible holds prayer and care together: elders who pray and anoint, figs on a king's boil, a doctor named as a friend.
what a scholar hears: when King Asa is faulted in his illness, it's because "he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians". some readers hear the fault in the not, not in the physicians.

notes: 'Oil, in that world, was also used as a medicine' and the trapdoor's 'oil was a common remedy in the ancient world' are background claims not stated in the cited text (Luke 10:34 shows it in use on wounds). Confirm or soften.
'Tradition holds that this same Luke wrote one of the Gospels': attributed to tradition; confirm phrasing.
1 Timothy is attributed to Paul in the text itself; some scholars question Pauline authorship. Lesson says 'Paul tells his young friend'. Confirm.
Anointing of the sick described as a sacrament in Catholic and Orthodox churches (howItsDone); confirm.
Lesson avoids any claim about faith-healing groups that refuse medicine; Keeper may want a gentle line about that, or not.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced background claim that oil was a medicine 'in that world' (spoken and trapdoor now lean only on Luke 10:34); softened 'a lot of families' to 'some families'; trimmed the Samaritan mention since day 1381 used the same story.

Audit: the Samaritan's oil and wine was still in the teach, a screen head, a myth and the trapdoor, repeating day 1381; replaced with Hezekiah's prayer heard and the fig plaster (Isaiah 38:5, 38:21). The myth 'the Bible treats going to a doctor as a lack of faith' was too broad given 2 Chronicles 16:12 (Asa); narrowed to Jesus, and the trapdoor now names Asa honestly. Keeper: confirm the 'fault in the not' reading of Asa is fair.
